Chemical injury: cleaning products, bleach, cement, lime, fertilisers or car battery acid splashing into the eye.
Something in the eye (foreign body): dust, sand, an insect or a small metal chip, especially when grinding or drilling.
Scratch on the cornea (corneal abrasion): from a fingernail, branch, paper or makeup brush. Very painful but usually heals in a few days with treatment.
Burns from light: looking at welding without a mask, or at the sun (including during an eclipse).
Rinse with plenty of clean water for chemicals or dust.
For a sharp injury, gently cover the eye with a paper cup or rigid shield without pressing on it, and go to Emergency.
For a blunt injury, a cold compress (ice wrapped in a cloth) can ease swelling. Do not press it hard on the eye.
Try not to eat or drink before seeing the doctor if the eye might need surgery.
try to pull out anything stuck in the eye
press on an eye that may be cut
put ointments, traditional remedies, breast milk or old eye drops in the eye
try to neutralise a chemical with another chemical (just use water)
Washing out the eye fully, and checking the pH (acid level) for chemical injuries.
Removing small particles from the surface of the eye.
Eye drops: antibiotics to prevent infection, drops to ease pain and inflammation, and drops to lower eye pressure if needed.
Surgery: to repair a cut or hole in the eye, remove an object from inside the eye, repair the eyelid, or fix a broken eye socket or detached retina.
A tetanus injection if needed, and follow-up visits.
Wear safety glasses for DIY, grinding, drilling, cutting grass and gardening.
Wear a proper welding mask for welding.
Wear eye protection for sports like badminton, squash and football.
Fireworks (mercun): keep children well away, and never lean over or relight a firework that has not gone off [4].
Store chemicals in their original containers, out of children's reach, and wear gloves and goggles when using strong cleaners.
Always wear a seatbelt in the car.
